newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Congress party begins search for new chief.
newsitem.headline: India's Congress party begins search for new chief.

text.p: The old guard of India's Congress party is fighting off the younger leaders and jousting with newcomers in a struggle to win the leadership of India's oldest political organisation.

The Congress party stepped up its search for a new president after former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao quit on Saturday when an Indian court upheld a summons ordering him to appear as a co-accused in a $100,000 cheating case.

"There is no front-runner to whom the party can be expected to automatically turn. There are three to four contenders, none of them adequate," said Pran Chopra, political analyst at the Centre for Policy Research, an independent think-tank.
The party's elite 19-member Congress Working Committee (CWC) will meet on Monday to elect a provisional new leader.

Rao, 74, had been under pressure from many of his party colleagues after he led Congress, which has ruled India for all but four years since independece in 1947, to its worst defeat in general elections this year.
A string of corruption scandals has dogged the Congress.
Seven of Rao's cabinet colleagues resigned early this year in a "bribes-for-favours" foreign exchange scandal.
Earlier this month the federal police arrested his communications minister over his controversial role in the award of contracts for telecommunications equipment.
Rao's decision to quit was welcomed by Congress dissidents, who had long sought his removal as party chief.

"Some unhappiness and apprehension was already there," Santosh Mohan Deb, a senior Congress leader and Rao loyalist, told Reuters. "Now the ball is in their court," he said, referring to the dissidents.
But party leaders admitted that the search for a new leader will not be easy.
Veteran Congress leaders like K. Karunakaran and Sharad Pawar are among the old guard most likely to jump into the leadership fray, analysts said.
Pranab Mukherjee, a former foreign minister and close confidant of Rao, is seen as another likely candidate.
But Chopra said Karunakaran had a distinct disadvantage as he lost in last May's parliamentary polls.
Many party members see Sharad Pawar, a former defence minister and chief minister of the country's wealthiest Maharashtra state, emerging as a top contender.
Congressmen who have broken away from the party may throw their weight behind the old guard, who could pave the way for their return to the Congress party, analysts said.
From among the younger leaders, the most likely contender will probably be Rajesh Pilot, a former junior interior minister in Rao's cabinet.
Pilot has spearheaded a campaign against corruption within the Congress party. But analysts say he's not popular.
"He has risen too fast and many Congressmen are wary of his ambitions," said a Congress leader who asked not to be named.
A section of the party seeks a clean new leadership to guide the it through its present crisis, analysts said.
One Congress leader who enjoys a clean image and public confidence is A.K. Antony, a former cabinet minister and ex-chief minister of the southern state of Kerala.
"But Antony's organisational capabilities are yet to proved," political analyst B.G. Verghese said.

Analysts said that Rao and his followers were unlikely to be content with the role of mere spectators in the succession struggle. With their majority in the CWC, they could push their own candidate, they said.
"Alternatively, we may well see a trend to consolidate and not fight among the party members," Verghese said.
